messages:
alex: Heads up - on prod-dedicated we've started seeing gradual GPU memory growth across long chat sessions (8-12h). Not an immediate OOM, but memory usage ticks up until cuda OOM on some hosts. Suspect allocator fragmentation vs a true leak. Repro + nvprof snapshot attached.

maria: Ugh. Any correlation with model size / seq len / kv cache policy? :thinking_face:

alex: Mostly with long seq and many unique conversation prefixes. KV cache hits are decent but we see many small allocations when we evict/refresh prefixes. Sequence len ~2048, batch 4-6.

jonathan: Can you paste the repro command you're using? Also which allocator (native vs cudaMallocAsync) and runtime flags?

alex: Repro is here:
```bash
python tools/repro/mem_run.py --model redwood/opt-1.3b --seq 2048 --batch 6 --iters 2000 --kv-mode incremental
```
We're running with torch + cudaMallocAsync enabled (CUDA 11.8 / driver 535). We also tried disabling async allocator and saw slightly different behavior.

paul: Did you try forcing workspace cap smaller? I remember a past regression where the workspace grew per request when cublasLt path switched and we kept allocating new temp buffers.

alex: Yes - tried workspace=512M (default), 256M, 128M. With 128M the long-term growth slows but doesn't disappear. Looks like some allocations aren't being returned to the pool.

kevin: Can you share a short profiler snapshot (nvtx/nvprof) where the growth is visible? nvprof traces + heap info would help distinguish fragmentation vs leak.

alex: Uploaded nvprof: nvprof_mem_1732104567.nvvp and a small cudaMalloc log:
``
[INFO] alloc 0x7f9b1c000000 64KB
[INFO] alloc 0x7f9b1c100000 128KB
[WARN] free 0x7f9b1c000000
[INFO] alloc 0x7f9b1c200000 64KB
[INFO] peak resident 10.1GB -> 11.6GB over 6h
```

maria: From that pattern it looks like many small alloc/free churn. If the allocator splits blocks and leaves tiny unusable fragments, you'd still see growing resident set. But a leak would show allocations never freed. Can you run a run with torch.cuda.memory_snapshot or using the new cudaMemPool APIs to dump pool state?

alex: Did a quick dump with torch.cuda.memory_summary() at t=0, t=2h, t=6h - summary shows increasing "inactive split" counts and declining "active blocks" being reusable. I'll attach the three snapshots.

jonathan: That strongly suggests fragmentation. Two mitigation paths: 1) coalesce smaller free blocks (allocator tuning), 2) prefer buffer reuse for KV cache entries by bucketing sizes to reduce mixed-size churn. Also consider enabling a persistent pooled KV cache that reuses buffers across conversations.

paul: On the runtime side we've seen a cublas kernel selection change when seq>1024 that allocates a temp workspace per forward that isn't returned until cudaStreamSynchronize due to our lazy GC. We might be holding onto temporary workspaces across requests in some edge cases.

kevin: Can we add metrics for "temporaries outstanding" and track workspace allocations per request id? If we see per-request temp count rising then we have a path bug.

alex: I'll add a lightweight counter and also flip a flag to force immediate cudaStreamSynchronize in a dev build to see if growth stops.

maria: For a quick experiment, try turning on cudaMallocAsync pool with a larger memory pool (cudaMemPoolSetAttribute) and enable reuse_buffers=True for the KV layer. If growth stops, it's fragmentation being masked by a bigger pool.

alex: Ran the experiments:
- Immediate sync: growth stopped - resident stable for 12h. :tada:
- cudaMallocAsync + larger pool: growth reduced but still slow creep.

jonathan: So there's at least one code path where we're delaying frees (hence the sync stops it). We should find that codepath and either ensure frees happen earlier or avoid allocating per-token workspace. Can you bisect back to recent runtime changes? Any PRs touching cublas workspace or kernel selection heuristics in the last 2 weeks?

alex: Two suspect PRs: #4929 (dynamic kernel selector for matmul path) and #5012 (lazy stream sync optimization). Both landed in the window.

paul: Repro script + profiler plus a patch that reverts the lazy sync optimization would be a good quick test. If reverting fixes, we need a safer gating or ensure workspace buffers are returned to pool on request completion.

kevin: Also, we should add an e2e perf test that runs long chat loops (8h-ish scaled down) to catch regressions. Add perf regression alert when peak resident increases >5% over baseline for same workload.

maria: For KV cache, implement bucketing: round-up allocations to nearest power-of-two class (or fixed size buckets) so reuse becomes effective. That tends to reduce fragmentation massively for small allocs.

alex: I'll push a dev build that reverts lazy sync and enables immediate pool coalescing. Attaching repro after patch: 1732104567-repro-after-revert.log. Please review.

jonathan: Nice. Also add unit that simulates concurrent eviction patterns so we trigger the same small-allocation churn.

paul: Filing follow-up tasks:
- ENGRT-314: revert lazy sync until we add stronger correctness checks (owner: jonathan)
- ENGRT-315: allocator tuning + bucketed KV allocations (owner: maria)
- ENGRT-316: long-run CI perf test and alert (owner: kevin)

alex: Thanks. I'll monitor prod after the revert rollout and post results here in 24h. :eyes:

sre-bot: Deployment green on pool-redwood-dedicated-34. Canary ran for 30m.

alex: Canary looked good for 30m; starting staged rollout now.

maria: If anyone needs the snapshots I pushed them to the perf bucket: s3://redwood-perf/nvvp/1732104567/

jonathan: Great work debugging everyone. We'll follow up on the buckets + allocator PRs after the immediate roll.

alex: Update - 24h after revert: no steady memory creep on the canary hosts. Rolling through all fleets. Will keep the tickets open for allocator improvements.

kevin: Awesome. Closing loop: add an incident postmortem note summarizing root cause (delayed frees from lazy sync + fragmentation amplification) and the short-term mitigation (revert lazy sync). Assign owners for permanent fixes.

alex: Will draft the postmortem and link here when ready.
